p: Friday, September 30, 2061. 6:40 AM. The simulator bay still smelled of last night: cold coffee, warm electronics, and the marker Rafa had used to write ONCE on the inside of the door, in letters a foot high. Sam had come in early to read the run logs before anybody could tell him what they meant. Somebody had beaten him to it.

Commander Yusra Haddad was in the left seat of the mockup with the lights down and the departure burn on the screen in front of her, flying it by hand. Ignition, nineteen minutes against the simulated Earth, cutoff. She reset it and flew it again. He stood at the back by the door, where she'd stood the night before, and counted. She flew it nine times. Nine for nine. On the last one she trimmed the burn a little late and then exactly right, the way the guidance had on run one, and he understood that she'd been watching the software last night as closely as it had been watching the ship.

She pulled the headset off and saw him. Rafa says once is a fact and twice is a capability, she said. I'm a capability. I've got a plane to Houston at ten. She picked up her bag. At the door she stopped and looked at the word on it for a while, and didn't say anything about it, and went.

Rafa's sixty engineers worked in two week sprints with a demo every other Friday. The autonomy squad was nine of them, at the software end of the cafeteria and the far end of the sim bay, and they'd built A1 in five sprints since July. Under ONCE, smaller, somebody had written the squad's velocity for each of those sprints in story points: 34, 28, 31, 37, 26. Nobody outside the squad had ever asked to see the column.
At 7:15 Rafa sent a page to Sam, Quinn, and Hana.

HALCYON FLIGHT SOFTWARE AUTONOMY A QUESTION FOR RELEASE A2 R. QUINTERO SEPTEMBER 30 2061. BUILD A1 FLEW THE DEPARTURE BURN IN SIM ONCE IN NINE RUNS. IT WAS BUILT TO HELP A CREW. IT TURNS OUT IT CAN NEARLY FLY ONE PART OF THE TRIP WITHOUT ONE.. QUESTION FOR THE PROGRAM: IF THE CREW CAN'T FLY IN THE WINDOW (AN INJURY, AN ILLNESS, A CREW LAUNCH THAT SLIPS PAST MARCH 4), CAN HALCYON GO ANYWAY, UNCREWED, AND DELIVER THE BREATHER?. TODAY THE ANSWER IS NO. THE BACKLOG HAS 1,140 ITEMS IN IT AND NONE OF THEM ASKS THAT QUESTION.. I'D LIKE TO ASK IT. I NEED SOMEBODY TO TELL ME WHAT GOES FIRST.

Garrett answered at 7:42, to everyone. Love the energy. The crew is the product. Let's not build a ship that makes the crew optional. At 8:05 Hale's chief of staff, who had been copied by somebody, wrote to Sam alone. The Director would like to understand whether Halcyon can "fly itself," and how soon she can say so.

Sam read both of them twice. Then he read the last line of Rafa's again. I need somebody to tell me what goes first. In nineteen years of running a building he had never once had to decide what mattered most in somebody else's software. He'd only had to keep the lights on while they decided.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 506.
Ruth's Console Log, page seven: good call.

Ruth's console log. Petrel Flow. L Minus 90 Days. March 14 2035. oh six thirty, fsw drop 7 is 9 days late. integrated sim slot is the 21ST. miss it and the rig goes to the cargo program until May. oh seven hundred, software lead: full regression is 60 hours on the rig. new tests only is 9. his numbers are good. he's been up since tuesday. oh seven ten, asked what full regression would find. he said probably nothing. wrote down probably. oh seven fifteen, approved new tests only. regression deferred to drop 8. my initials. oh seven forty, tate: did anyone rerun the abort sequence. lead: it didn't change. tate: the thing next to it did. oh seven forty one, told tate to put it in writing. she did. filed it for drop 8. March 21 0900 sim. drop 7 flew clean, all phases. March 21 0930 administrator on the loop: good call, ruthie. March 21 1700 L minus 83. good call. writing it down so I remember what it felt like.

Good call, Ruthie. I wrote it down so I'd remember what it felt like, and I can tell you exactly what it felt like, because I've had twenty six years to think about it. It felt wonderful. The drop was late, the sim slot was going to the cargo program, the software lead hadn't slept since Tuesday, and I found nine hours where there had been sixty. The sim was clean. The Administrator said my name on the loop. I drove home with the radio on.

That's the worst thing that can happen to a bad decision. It works. Drop 8's regression was deferred to drop 9, because drop 7 had flown clean without one. Drop 9's was deferred to the launch load. Roz Tate's note about the thing next to the abort sequence went into a file for drop 8 and stayed in it. And in May, when Wendell's third retest of the valve came up against the schedule, I'd already learned three times that skipping the expensive check costs nothing. You've read page four. You'll get to page nine. This is the page where I learned how to sign it.

Roz was right, for the record. The investigation board went through every drop line by line in 2036, and in drop 7 it found a timer in the abort sequence counting one cycle late, from a change two files over. It had nothing to do with June 12. It flew in the load we launched, it never fired, and nobody knew it was there until a board read the code afterward. I think about the day it would have fired more than I think about most things.

This page is mostly three tasks. R3 is value-based delivery, R2 is scope, and R7 is quality. There's a good deal of R9 and B6 in it too. The software on your ship is agile, and I'm glad. Agile is very good at something I was bad at, which is finding out early. It has the same weak spot I had, though. When the date pushes, the first thing anybody offers to cut is the check that would have told you the truth.
How the exam asks it. When a scenario offers to protect a date by skipping testing or review, the answer protects quality and changes scope or schedule through the people who own them.

The ECO's R3 task is to help ensure value-based delivery, and its enablers read like the questions you should ask before anyone writes a line. Identify the value components with key stakeholders. Prioritize work by value and stakeholder feedback. Look for chances to deliver value incrementally. Keep examining the business value as you go. Make sure there's a way to measure the benefit. Evaluate delivery options to demonstrate value. None of them says build what you were asked for. All of them say find out what it's for.

A minimum viable product is the agile world's way of asking what it's for as cheaply as possible. The usual definition is a version with just enough features to be usable by early customers, who then tell you what to build next. On a Mars ship you don't get early customers, so I'd put it the way an engineer would: the smallest thing that works end to end and answers the question you're most afraid of. An MVP isn't a cheap copy of the product. It's an experiment in the product's shape. If it leaves out a whole phase of the mission, it can't tell you anything about the mission.

Here's the part that matters on your program. Some of the most valuable work a project does produces something you hope you'll never use. A backup. A contingency mode. A second way through a window. Its value isn't in using it. Its value is what not having it would cost, times the chance you'll need it. You did that arithmetic on page four with a test article, and an option is the same sum. When the cost of not having it is the window, the option can be worth more than half the features anybody asked for, and the honest way to fund it is to say so out loud: write it down as an option, show what it displaces, and take it through change control where everyone can see it.

And watch the word output. A team can produce a great deal of output and very little value: features nobody needs, points that don't fly. Value is what the stakeholders get. Output is what the team did. They're related the way miles driven and arriving are related.

How the exam asks it. If an answer builds the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption and gets feedback on it, it's usually right. Building everything first, or the easy parts first, is usually the distractor.

The product backlog is the ordered list of everything the product might need. It isn't a requirements document and it isn't a queue of requests. It's ordered, somebody has to do the ordering, and that somebody is the product owner. The Scrum Guide is short about it: the product owner is one person, not a committee. They may represent the needs of many stakeholders, and anyone who wants to change the backlog can do it by trying to convince them. The developers size the work. The product owner owns the order and answers for the value.

Why one person? Because a list ordered by a committee is a list ordered by whoever was loudest that week, and a list ordered by the people building it drifts toward what's interesting to build. Neither of those is wicked. Both are how a team ends up with a beautiful guidance loop and nothing that lands.

Refinement is the ongoing work of breaking big items into smaller and clearer ones, adding detail, and sizing them, so the top of the list is always ready to plan. Most teams do some every sprint, a few hours at a time. The top of the list should be small and sharp. The bottom can be vague. Nobody should spend a day detailing something that may never get built.

Then the ordering. You'll meet two tools. MoSCoW sorts items into must have, should have, could have, and won't have this time. Dai Clegg came up with it in 1994 for work with a fixed deadline, which describes every project you'll ever run. The musts are sometimes called the minimum usable subset: if one of them is missing, the release has failed. Weighted shortest job first gives you an order. Add up an item's cost of delay, which is its value to the user or the business, its time criticality, and the risk it retires or the opportunity it opens, and divide by its size. Small, urgent, risky work rises. Big work sinks, sometimes too far, which is why you use the two together. The formula knows arithmetic. The product owner knows what the release is for.

Technical debt goes on the same list. Ward Cunningham, who named it in 1992, said shipping first time code is like going into debt, and a little debt speeds development so long as it's paid back promptly. A known defect left in to make a date is debt, and every sprint you build on top of it you pay interest. Put it where the product owner can see it and weigh it. It usually ranks higher than anybody expected.

How the exam asks it. Who orders the backlog? The product owner. Who sizes the items? The developers. A stakeholder who wants something moved talks to the product owner. WSJF divides cost of delay by size, and the highest score goes first.

Sprint planning starts with why: a sprint goal, one sentence about what the sprint is for. Then what: the items from the top of the backlog that serve the goal. Then how: the developers' plan for doing them. The whole team builds that plan, and the product owner makes sure the most important items are ready to talk about.

How much fits is a question about capacity and velocity. Velocity is how many points a team actually finishes in a sprint, counted against the definition of done, averaged over the last several. Capacity is who's actually there: holidays, training, a week on another shift. If a team of nine averages thirty points and two of the ten days are holidays, it has eighty percent of its capacity and should plan about eighty percent of its points. Story points are a size relative to other items, not hours. That's why one team's thirty isn't another team's thirty, and why comparing teams by velocity is one of the quickest ways to make velocity useless.

Velocity is a planning tool. The moment it becomes a target, people get better at estimating generously and the number stops telling you anything. That's Goodhart's law, and engineers are subject to it like everyone else. Use velocity to forecast, and forecast as a range. Take the average for the most likely, take the slow and fast ends of the recent sprints for the edges, and divide the remaining backlog by each. Round up, because a team finishes in whole sprints. Say what the forecast assumes, mainly that the backlog won't grow much. Update it every sprint. A single date from velocity is page three over again, one number with the uncertainty sanded off.

Once a sprint starts, its goal is protected. The Scrum Guide says that during the sprint no changes are made that would endanger the goal, quality does not decrease, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the product owner as more is learned. Read those together. When a sprint runs into trouble, the thing that bends is scope, with the product owner. Quality doesn't bend. Neither does the timebox, much, because everyone else plans around it.

How the exam asks it. Forecasts from velocity are ranges. An answer that uses the best sprint ever, or gives one date with no range, is a distractor. When a sprint is in trouble, renegotiate scope with the product owner. Don't cut quality and don't stretch the sprint.

A burndown chart plots the work remaining against time: points up the side, days along the bottom, and a straight line from the commitment down to zero that people call the ideal line, although it's only arithmetic on an estimate. The useful part is the actual line and where it sits. Below the ideal, the team's ahead. Above it, behind. The slope is the burn rate.

Learn the shapes. A line that stays flat for days usually means work is getting finished but not getting to done, which is the most common way a sprint goes wrong and the hardest one to see on a status slide. A line that steps up means work was added. A line that falls off a cliff on the last day means the team was holding items until the end, and often means the definition of done got thinner on Thursday night.

A burnup chart shows the same story with two lines: work completed, climbing, and total scope, which should be flat and often isn't. When the lines meet, you're done. When scope grows as fast as completion, you never are, and a burnup shows it where a burndown hides it. For reporting a release to anyone outside the team I prefer the burnup. It makes scope growth a fact instead of a feeling.

Say a sprint commits forty points over ten days. The ideal burn is four a day. At the end of day six the ideal remaining is sixteen, and the team has twenty two left. Through six days it has finished eighteen, three a day. At three a day it finishes twelve more in the last four days and ends with ten points undone. That's the conversation to have with the product owner on day six, while there's something to decide.

How the exam asks it. A flat burndown means work isn't reaching done, or work is being added as fast as it's finished. For scope growth, look at a burnup's top line. The action is nearly always a conversation with the product owner about scope.

Two lists get confused, and the exam knows it. Acceptance criteria belong to one item. They say what that story must do to be accepted: the lander reports touchdown within ten minutes. The definition of done belongs to every item. It's the quality bar the whole increment has to clear: reviewed, tested, integrated, whatever the product needs. An item has to meet both. The Scrum Guide calls the definition of done a formal description of the state of the increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, and it's strict about the consequence. An item that doesn't meet it can't be released or even presented at the sprint review. It goes back to the backlog.

For safety critical software the definition has to reach past the team's own edge. Verification asks whether you built the product right, against its specification. Validation asks whether you built the right product, for what it's for. Both need the real system, or the best model of it you have: an integrated simulation with the hardware models in it, and not only unit tests on a developer's machine. They need regression, because the oldest way to break working code is to change the code beside it. And they need somebody independent.

Independent verification and validation means a team that had nothing to do with building the software checks it, and it's independent three ways: its money, its management, and its technical judgment don't come from the people whose work it checks. Space agencies, aviation regulators, and defense programs use it because people are bad at finding the faults in their own reasoning. Coverage is the other word you'll hear. Statement coverage asks whether every line ran in a test. Branch coverage asks whether every decision went both ways. Safety critical work often requires something stricter, modified condition and decision coverage, which shows that every condition in a decision can change the outcome on its own. You won't be asked to compute it. You may be asked why one hundred percent of lines isn't the same as tested.
Done costs capacity, and you plan for it. When integrated sim and regression are in the definition, the team's velocity is lower, and it's lower because it's true.

How the exam asks it. Meets its acceptance criteria but not the definition of done: not done, and back to the backlog. For safety critical software, done includes integration, regression, and independent review, and the team plans its capacity around them.

The 2026 ECO names artificial intelligence as one of the trends PMI fed into the analysis behind the exam, and you've met it twice in my pages: a schedule on page three, and now code. The rule is the same both times. An AI tool's output is an input. It can be very good. It isn't evidence.

The vendors say so themselves. One assistant's own documentation calls hallucination a known risk of these models and a key reason human review of AI generated output is important. Hallucination is output that sounds plausible and is unsupported or made up. The subtler trap is the tests. If the same tool writes the code and the tests from the same example, they share the same assumptions. The tests will agree with the code because they came from the same place, and agreement between two things with one source isn't verification. It's an echo.

So treat generated code the way you'd treat code from a contractor you've never worked with. Mark it, so everyone knows where it came from. Have a named person review it who can explain every line of it, numbers included. Write or check its tests from the requirement, independently. Keep the things that must have one value, constants and limits, in one place, and never let anyone, person or tool, type them in from memory. And remember who's accountable. The tool doesn't sign anything. The person who accepted the code owns it, and the process that let it through owns the rest.

Banning the tool is the tempting answer after a bad week, and it's usually wrong. People make the same mistakes, only slower. Fix the review and the tests, and then decide what the tool is good for. It's good for a lot.

How the exam asks it. AI output in a scenario is an input to verify. The best answer reviews and tests it independently and keeps a person accountable. Trusting it as it comes and banning it outright are both distractors.

Defects will come, from people and tools and the gaps between them. What you do in the first day decides whether you learn anything. Found how: write it down, because how you found it tells you which of your checks worked. Contained how: stop it going further, then look for the same cause everywhere it could have reached, because a defect that came from a process exists wherever that process ran. Root cause: keep asking why until you reach something you can change in how the work gets done. A person is almost never the root cause. A person is where the cause became visible.

Then report it, honestly, early, through the path the program set up. The Code's 5.2.3 asks for accurate information in a timely manner, and 5.3.1 rules out withholding information that would make what we say misleading. A defect the team reports before anybody asks is evidence the system works. The same defect found by somebody else is evidence it doesn't, and everyone will read it that way.

The retrospective is where the team changes how it works. The Scrum Guide says it inspects how the sprint went, including the definition of done, and that the assumptions that led the team astray get identified and their origins explored. Run it blameless. One engineering organization that writes about this a great deal says a blameless review focuses on the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, because where finger pointing and shaming prevail, people stop bringing problems to light for fear of punishment. That isn't kindness. It's how you keep your own program's information coming to you.

Last, B6, continuous improvement: use the lessons learned, keep the improvement processes current, and update the organizational process assets. A lesson that lives in one project's register helps one project, for a while. A lesson that changes the company's standard, its checklist, its template, helps every team that comes after, including the ones who've never heard of you. That's where the fix belongs.
That's page seven. It worked. Be careful with the ones that work.

How the exam asks it. After a defect: contain it, find the root cause in the process, report it honestly through the defined path, and update the organization's standards. Blaming the individual, hiding it until it's fixed, and banning the tool are the distractors.

Monday, October 3. The flight software backlog lived in a tool on Rafa's laptop and, more and more, in Rafa's head. Eleven hundred and forty items. Quinn had pulled the request history for September and printed it out on the big room table, and the printout hung off both ends.

Requests came from everywhere. The Director's office had added nine items in September, all marked high. Garrett had added four through his assistant, all marked urgent, one of them a boot screen with the mission patch on it. Hana had added two about the valve model. Okonkwo's station engineers had added six about the Breather's alarms, through the morning packet. Commander Haddad had added thirty one, all from demos, every one a thing that would have killed her. Rafa had ordered all of it himself, at night, and reordered it whenever somebody senior walked past his desk.
I build it, he said. I shouldn't also be the one who decides what it's for. I've been doing both and I'm doing the second one badly.
Garrett, on the speaker from his car: Then you decide, Sam. Program manager. One throat to choke.

Sam didn't think it should be his throat. He thought it should be the person who'd have to sit on the ship. At noon he called Haddad in Houston, on the first full day of a week of training, and asked her. She said yes before he'd finished asking. Then she asked what she'd be the owner of, exactly. Who can change my order? And who gets to call you when they don't like it?
Her calendar for October had eleven free hours in it.
Haddad said yes, then asked who can change her order. How should Sam set up her role?
A. Make Haddad product owner, with each change to her order cleared by Garrett's office and the Director's.
B. Name Haddad product owner, and let Rafa keep the day to day ordering while she's in Houston.
C. Make Haddad the one person who orders the backlog, and get her the hours the job needs.
D. Make Haddad and Rafa joint product owners, Haddad for crew items and Rafa for technical ones.

He writes it on one page that afternoon and sends it to every lead and to the Director's office. Who orders the backlog: Haddad, and only Haddad. Who can ask: anyone, by convincing her. Who sizes: the developers. What Sam does: clears her calendar and backs her when somebody senior calls. Then he spends Tuesday with the crew office in Houston and gets her two days a week at Watkins through March, which also means two nights a week at home in Aurora. She sends one line about that. My husband says thank you. So do I. Rafa prints the Scrum Guide's sentence about convincing the product owner and tapes it to his monitor. I'm going to enjoy reading that to Garrett.

That's a go. A product backlog needs one owner who answers for its value and orders it on behalf of every stakeholder, while the developers size the work and decide how to do it. Establish the roles clearly, give the owner the time and the authority, and stand behind her.

Tuesday, October 4. Haddad had been product owner for one day, and her first act was a question she sent to Sam, Rafa, Quinn, and Hana at 6:02 AM from a hotel in Houston. Before I order anything: what is the autonomy release for? I need one sentence.
Nobody had one. They had four.

Rafa's was everything: every phase of the flight, every fault the ship could have, a crew optional ship by the end of 2062. Garrett's was the sentence he'd already said to his investors on Friday afternoon, Halcyon can fly itself, the same three words Hale's chief of staff had used that morning. Hana's was quieter. She'd rather the squad spent the year on the crew's displays and the valve model, the things the crew would actually use, and let the uncrewed idea sit in a drawer. Nobody's going to fly my stage without a crew on it, she said. That's a slide.

Quinn's wasn't a sentence. It was arithmetic. The crew launched up to the ship in January 2063. If they couldn't go, for any reason, an injury, an illness, a crew launch that slipped, the window closed on March 4 with the Breather still circling the Earth. On the worst number anybody had, the colony couldn't wait twenty six months for the next one. On the agency's own number it couldn't either.
Quinn had written it on a sticky note and stuck it to Sam's monitor. WHAT IF THE CREW CAN'T GO?
The program's change board met on Wednesdays.
Quinn's sticky note asks what happens if the crew can't go. What should Sam do with that question?
A. Size the smallest uncrewed version that still lands the Breather, and take it to Wednesday's change board.
B. Have Haddad add the uncrewed work to the backlog, and order it against the rest as product owner.
C. Let Hale tell the partners that Halcyon can fly itself, in the words Garrett gave his investors.
D. Keep the uncrewed idea out of the release, as Hana suggests, and spend the year on crew displays.

They write the sentence together on the big room whiteboard, Haddad on the screen from Houston. Release A2 makes it possible for Halcyon to fly the Breather to Mars and land it without a crew, if it has to, by the time the crew would have to commit to fly. Under it, what the smallest version must do: depart, coast, correct, capture at Mars, hand off the lander, land it. Crude in every phase, whole from one end to the other. Quinn and the squad size it at 286 points. It fits inside the software release plan if the crew display work moves later, so the change is to the release plan and the integrated plan and not to the budget, and on Wednesday it goes to the change board with what moves, what it costs the crew, and what the program gets for it: a second way through the window. The board approves it with one condition, Hana's. It's written down everywhere as an option, and never as the plan. Haddad reads the minutes and sends one line. Approved. I'll order it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Value-based delivery asks what the work is for, and an option you hope never to use can be the most valuable thing on the list when the cost of not having it is the window. Define the minimum that answers the question, weigh it against what it displaces, and take it through change control in the open.

Thursday, October 6. Quinn had booked the big room for the day and covered one wall in brown paper. Rafa's squad of nine stood in front of it with sticky notes, wearing the expressions of engineers who'd been told this would be fun.
The change board had approved the uncrewed option on Wednesday, as an option, in writing. Now somebody had to turn one sentence into work that a squad could finish two weeks at a time.

Haddad was on the screen from Houston with sticky notes of her own, which she held up to the camera one at a time. Overnight the station engineers had sent a packet listing what a lander would have to tell them after it touched down, and the list was longer than anyone at Watkins had expected.

Garrett's idea arrived at 8 AM, forwarded with no comment. Have Furrow do it. It'll write the stories overnight. Furrow was the code assistant Tallgrass had licensed for every engineer in July. It wrote code, it wrote tests, and according to the vendor's brochure it wrote user stories.
Garrett wants Furrow to write the stories overnight. How should the release be broken down?
A. Write a full specification for the release, and get every requirement signed before more building.
B. Slice the release into thin end to end versions of every phase, flown in sim before any is thickened.
C. Have Furrow draft the stories overnight from the release sentence, and import them in the morning.
D. Break the release down by layer, guidance through fault handling, finishing each before the next.

By four the wall has a spine across the top, one card per phase: depart, coast, correct, capture, hand off, land. Under each phase the cards get better as they go down, crude at the top and good at the bottom. The first row, the thinnest version of everything, is one sprint of work if they're lucky and two if they're honest. Every card has its acceptance criteria on the back in Haddad's words or the station's. Lander reports touchdown, attitude, and Breather bay temperature within ten minutes of landing. Rafa looks at the top row for a long time. That's a ship that's bad at everything. It's a ship that does everything, Haddad says. Badly. Then you make it good, and I watch.

Exactly right. Break scope down so each piece works end to end and can be tested, then improve it in increments. Write acceptance criteria with the people who'll use the product. Thin vertical slices show you the whole problem early, while there's still time to learn from it.

Friday, October 7. Backlog refinement, the squad's word for the afternoon when they sat down with the product owner and argued about what was worth what. Haddad flew in that morning and came straight from the airport with her bag still on her shoulder.
At the top of the list were five items everybody agreed mattered and nobody agreed how much.

RELEASE A2 REFINEMENT TOP FIVE, NOT YET ORDERED. TIMING RACE IN THE GUIDANCE LOOP. KNOWN DEFECT FROM A1. FAILED RUN 2 ON SEPTEMBER 29.. SAFE MODE ON LOSS OF SIGNAL: HOLD ATTITUDE, KEEP THE BREATHER STACKS WARM, WAIT FOR THE GROUND.. TERMINAL DESCENT: HOVER AND TRANSLATE TO THE SITE.. BURN SUMMARY ON THE CREW DISPLAY AFTER CUTOFF. REQUESTED BY Y. HADDAD.. INVESTOR REPLAY MODE FOR RUN ONE, WITH NARRATION. REQUESTED BY THE OFFICE OF THE CEO.

Rafa wanted the descent first, because it was the hardest, and hard things were the fun ones. The two engineers who'd found the timing race wanted it fixed first, and said so in the tone people use when they've said a thing three times. Garrett's office had called twice about the replay mode, which had a date attached to it, because the investors met on November 15.
Haddad put her own card, the burn summary, face down on the table. Don't let me win because I'm holding the pen, she said. Tell me what each one costs us for every sprint we don't have it.
Five items top the list, and everyone but Haddad wants their own first. How should the backlog be ordered?
A. Put the Director's and the CEO's requests at the top, and order the rest of the list beneath them.
B. Start with the terminal descent, the hardest item and the one carrying the most technical risk.
C. Score each item's cost of delay with Haddad and the squad, then divide it by the item's size.
D. Clear the two small items first, the burn summary and the replay mode, then take on the rest.

They score on the whiteboard, three columns for cost of delay and one for size. The timing race, small and in the way of everything, comes out on top by a mile. Safe mode second. The descent fourth on the raw score, behind Haddad's own summary. Haddad looks at that for a while and then does the thing Sam later writes to Ruth about. She marks the descent a must have for the release and her summary a should have, and moves her own card down below it. The formula's right about the order, she says. It doesn't know what the release is for. I do. The replay mode goes in as a won't have this time, with a note to Garrett's office explaining why, which Sam signs.

That's a go. Prioritize by value and risk: cost of delay adds what an item is worth, how fast that value decays, and the risk it retires, and dividing by size brings quick, important work forward. MoSCoW sets what the release must contain. Technical debt that blocks everything belongs at the top.

Monday, October 10. Sprint planning for A2-1, the release's first sprint, in the sim bay at 8 AM. By nine the squad had a sprint goal on the board, the guidance loop runs without the race, and the ship can keep itself safe when the ground goes quiet, and a forecast of thirty points, against a capacity Quinn had worked out to the person day.
Then they got to the definition of done, and Thandi Mokoena stood up.

Mokoena led the ARA's independent verification and validation team for Halcyon's software: five people in a trailer behind the sim bay, paid by the ARA, reporting to the agency's mission assurance office and to nobody at Tallgrass, which was the whole point of them. She'd been at the back of the room for all nine A1 runs, writing.
AUTONOMY SQUAD DEFINITION OF DONE REV 4 MAY 2061. CODE REVIEWED BY ONE OTHER SQUAD MEMBER.. UNIT TESTS WRITTEN AND PASSING.. MERGED TO THE RELEASE BRANCH.. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA MET.
Everything on that list happens inside the squad, she said. Nothing on it happens on the ship. A1 was done by this definition on September 23, and it flew once in nine. I'd like done to mean flown.
The integrated sim is a six hour run, Rafa said. Full regression is twenty two hours on the rig. Put that in done and half our points stop being done.
Rafa says a stricter done would undo half their points. What should done include?
A. Write an integrated sim run, an independent review, and full regression into done for every item.
B. Add an integrated sim run to done for guidance stories only, and keep the rest on unit tests.
C. Leave done as written, and add an integrated sim run to the acceptance criteria where it's needed.
D. Keep done as written, and leave integrated sim and independent testing to the integration team.

They rewrite it on the board. Rev 5 adds three lines: flown in the integrated sim against the stage and Breather models, with the run logged; reviewed against the requirement by someone outside the squad, from Mokoena's team; full regression passed on the rig. The forecast stays at thirty, because Mokoena's people run the reviews and the rig runs at night, but nothing counts until its logs are in, and Rafa says that's going to make Fridays very tense, and then says, more slowly, that it's the first definition he'd want on a ship his own kids were watching. Mokoena books the rig for every Wednesday night through March. Haddad, from the back, asks for one thing: that rev 5 be printed and posted in the sim bay where the crew trains, so they know what done means on their ship.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. For safety critical software the definition of done should hold the quality measures the product needs: integration with models of the real system, independent verification, and regression. It applies to every item, the team plans capacity around it, and nothing counts until it's met.

Saturday, October 15. Haddad's youngest played under eight soccer on Saturday mornings at a park in Aurora eleven blocks from Sam's house, which he hadn't known until she texted him a field number and asked if he'd come by. Field 6. Orange slices in a cooler. A man in a folding chair with a bullhorn he didn't need.

She stood on the sideline in a Halcyon fleece with her hands in her pockets and watched a seven year old in shin guards bigger than his legs miss the ball three times in a row with enormous confidence. That's Idris. He's going to be a goalkeeper. He doesn't know yet.

They watched for a while. Then, without looking at him: I ordered the uncrewed work last week. I put it where it goes. I'm good at my job. A whistle went. So I'd like you to tell me something, and I'd like it to be true. Are you planning to fly my ship without me?
Sam thought about the answer he'd have liked to give. Then he thought about a flight line in Arizona, a long time ago, and a signature he'd have given a lot for one more hour on.
Haddad asks whether anyone is planning to fly her ship without her. How should Sam answer?
A. Reassure her it's a software exercise, and that the program won't fly Halcyon without its crew.
B. Tell her flying uncrewed is the board's call and the Director's, and offer to set up that meeting.
C. Tell her it's a real contingency, and ask her to keep it from her crew until the board decides.
D. Tell her it's for the day the crew can't go, and ask her to write the rule for when it's used.

We're planning for the day we'd have to, ma'am. You break an ankle in January. A launch slips past March 4. The station can't wait twenty six months while we find you a replacement. You're the plan. This is what happens if the plan can't go. She doesn't say anything for long enough that Idris misses the ball again. Okay, she says. Then I'd like to write the rule for when it gets used. Before anybody needs it. With my crew. He says yes. On Monday there's a new card in her handwriting at the top of the backlog's governance column. CRITERIA FOR AN UNCREWED DEPARTURE. OWNER: HADDAD, WITH THE CREW AND THE BOARD. And under it, smaller: Written before we know the answer.

Exactly right. Identify what the stakeholder actually expects and fears, tell her the truth about the plan, and bring her into the decision that affects her most. Aligning expectations means facilitating that conversation, and the criteria, with the people who'll live with them, before the pressure arrives.
Decision seven. Who brings the doctor.

Monday, October 17. 5:40 AM. The two note chime. One way light time fourteen minutes and three seconds. He'd recorded his own log to her on Saturday night, after Field 6, and hadn't checked his hands.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3790. One way, 14 minutes 3 seconds. Margin, 680 days. Hi, Dad. Sol 3790. I have a guest. Say hi, Malik. He says hi. He's waving. He's nineteen and he waves like he's bringing in a plane. Malik's on my night shift now, Bay A and Bay C and, when nobody's looking, the other place. He's very good with the pumps and very bad with the plants. He talks to them. He says they like it. They do not like it, Malik. The basil is dying of your opinions. We made you a cooking show. This is Malik's recipe. One jalapeño. That's the recipe. There's a first green one on the plants I put in for Mom, and he wants to eat it, and I said he can have half if he says something nice about it on camera, so you'll know. Go. He says it's the best thing he's eaten in two years. Now he's crying, which is the jalapeño. Now he's coughing, which isn't. Okay. Go do the pumps. He's gone. I'll tell you now, because he made me promise not to tell his mom, and you're not his mom. He's had that cough for three weeks. Medical says it's the dust and the dry air in the night bays, and they're probably right. The good inhalers ran out in July. So he has the other kind, and it's fine, and he says it's fine, and at three in the morning I listen to him from the next bay. Don't tell Frances. I mean it, Dad. It's his to tell. But she's going to call you about something, she always does, and when she does you'll know this, and I'm sorry. Something else. Okonkwo's people listen to the loop recordings, the copies of Earth's voice loops that come up a day late in the morning packet, and on one of them they heard that Earth's building a ship that can fly itself. Half the station heard no doctor. The crew's bringing Dr. Rao, and everybody up here knows her name. If the ship can come without her, people want to know who decides that. I watched yours twice. You've got orange on your thumb. I want to know whose soccer game that was. 680. Same minus nine. Love you. Ada out.

He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on Malik's face in the middle of a laugh, because Frances had held a photograph of that face against her coat at the back of a briefing room in February, and in the photograph he'd been sixteen and had never coughed.
At 9:10 Frances Odum called his cell. She didn't say hello. She never had.
It had started on the station, from a loop recording, and come down to Earth in the families' messages.

There's a story going around the families that the ship can come without its crew. Malik says the station's heard it too. I've got two hundred families asking me one thing, Mr. Okafor. If it comes without them, who brings the doctor?
A pause, and then the thing he'd been afraid she would say. And is there anything up there I should know about? Anything about my son?
Frances asks who brings the doctor, and whether there's anything about her son. How should Sam answer?
A. Tell her gently about Malik's three week cough, and that medical thinks it's the dust.
B. Answer the doctor question, say he can't speak for Malik, and suggest she ask him.
C. Answer the doctor question, and tell her he can't discuss an individual colonist's health.
D. Tell her the crew is flying with Dr. Rao, and that the uncrewed mode is a software exercise.

The crew is the plan, ma'am, and Dr. Rao is on the crew. We've looked hard at a way to get the plant there if the crew can't go, because the colony can't wait for the next window. If it's ever used, the board decides, on criteria written down before anybody needs them, and you'll hear it from me the same day. A breath. About your son. I can't speak for the station. I'd ask him. I'd ask him how he is, on a day when you've got time to hear the whole answer. The line is quiet for a long time. You know something, Frances says. I know he's the one to ask. That night he records a log to Ada and tells her Frances called, and what he said, and that he thinks Malik should be the one to tell her, and soon.

That's a go. Manage an external stakeholder's expectations with what you can honestly stand behind: what's planned, what the option is for, who decides, and when she'll hear. A third person's private information stays his. You can still point her to the person who can tell her, and tell your source what you said.

Wednesday, October 26. The October quarterly estimate was due to the partners on Monday the 31st, and Hale's chief of staff had called on Tuesday to ask for one line in it. The chief of staff's email came an hour later, so there'd be a record. The Director would like a date for the autonomy release that she can give the partners with confidence.
The option was in the release plan, declared, with Hana's word on it. The partners had read the word option, and now they wanted to know when.

The quarterly would carry the program's estimate at completion of 2,600 again, the number the Rule 4.2 notice had carried in July, against a budget of 2,472. The partners had funded the year's next tranche in August and would take up anything above the baseline against this estimate.

Quinn had the squad's numbers on one page. Five of the six sprints were measured under the old definition of done, she said. Rev 5 costs points. Whatever range I give you, read it wider than it looks.

Autonomy squad velocity, last six sprints (story points). Release A2 has 256 points left at the start of A2-2, Monday, October 24, refined and sized by the squad. Two week sprints, each ending on a Friday; A2-2 ends November 4.
Garrett had looked at it over Quinn's shoulder on his way past. Thirty seven. They did thirty seven once. Use that and put it in January. Partners love January.
Garrett wants the forecast built on the squad's best sprint. What should Sam forecast?
A. Forecast a range from the squad's slowest and fastest recent sprints, with its assumptions.
B. Forecast the date from the squad's best sprint so far, thirty seven points, as Garrett suggests.
C. Forecast one date from the squad's average velocity, and say it'll be updated as they learn.
D. Leave the autonomy line out of the quarterly until the squad has finished the release.

Quinn writes the line herself and Sam signs it. Release A2: most likely Friday, February 24, 2062. Range February 10 to March 10, from the squad's last six sprints. Assumes the backlog doesn't grow. Growth or light holiday sprints push it toward March 10. Updated every second Friday, after the sprint review. Hale's chief of staff calls back to say the Director would prefer one date. Sam says he understands, that this is the line he can stand behind, and that the next update is November 4. Then Hale comes on the line herself. Then I'll say a range, she says. I've said worse things to eleven governments.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Velocity is a planning tool, and an honest forecast from it is a range: the slow sprints and the fast ones, the scope assumptions, and when it will be updated. Communicate status in a form decision makers can use, and keep updating it as the data come in.
Tuesday, November 1. 9:40 PM. Sam was in his truck in the lot with the engine running when Mokoena called.

Under rev 5 the rig flew stories in the integrated sim on Wednesday nights, and on a Tuesday when the squad asked, for a story that wanted to be done by Friday. Tonight it was the first version of the terminal descent hover, merged on October 26. The squad's own tests were green. The story was one integrated run from done.

In the sim, the lander came down through the thin Martian air to four hundred meters, where the profile called for a hover, and didn't hover. It climbed. It climbed away from the landing site on seventy nine percent throttle, where Mars needed thirty, and ran out of propellant eleven hundred meters up, and fell.
By eleven Mokoena's team had found the line. In a routine called descent hover trim, one constant, G local, set to 9.80665. Standard gravity. Earth's, to six figures. Mars was about 3.73.

The routine had been written by Furrow. The engineer who'd asked for it, a guidance engineer eleven months on the program, had given it the hover code from the lander's tether tests at Watkins as an example, and it had done exactly what it was shown. It had also written the unit tests, from the same example, with the same number in them, and every one of them passed. One squad member had reviewed the merge. Mokoena's review was booked for Thursday, after the integrated run, which was the order rev 5 put them in.

The engineer was in the sim bay when Sam got there, sitting on the floor against the rig with his badge in both hands. Garrett had already texted from somewhere with music behind it. Was this the AI thing? Fix it tonight, don't make it a story.
A Furrow routine flew an Earth number, and Garrett says fix it tonight. What should Sam do first?
A. Ban Furrow from flight code tonight, and have the squad rewrite by hand everything it produced since July.
B. Pull the routine, and have Mokoena's team search all of Furrow's flight code for the same Earth assumption.
C. Fix the constant tonight, add a unit test for it, and log it as a defect in the squad's tracker.
D. Have the engineer who accepted the routine re-review all of his merged code for Earth values this week.

By morning Mokoena's team and the squad have read every line Furrow wrote since July and found four more uses of 9.80665. Two are right, in the engine model, where standard gravity is how you turn specific impulse into thrust and is supposed to be Earth's. One is wrong, in a parachute deployment check nobody had flown yet. One is a comment. The routine comes out of the release branch at 2 AM. The corrected version, with the constant taken from the program's single constants file and tests written from the requirement by someone who didn't write the code, goes back in on Thursday. Sam writes the defect report himself at seven on Wednesday morning and sends it to the board's clerk and Hale's office before nine: what failed, how it was found, what's contained, what isn't known yet. The last line says the code was written by an AI assistant and accepted by people, and that the program's process let both of those happen. Then he finds the engineer, who's still in the building, and tells him what he wrote.

Exactly right. When a defect is found, contain it first, then look for the same cause everywhere it could be, report it honestly through the defined path, and fix the process that let it through. AI generated code is an input: it needs the same human review and independent testing as anything else, and the people who accept it own it.

Thursday, November 3. 7:30 AM. Day nine of A2-2. The sprint review was Friday at two, with Haddad in the left seat and the readiness board's clerk in the back row, because the board had asked to see an autonomy increment at its November session and wanted a look first.
By Wednesday morning Mokoena's team and the squad had read every line Furrow had written since July. The parachute check was fixed too, and the defect report was with the board's clerk.
Quinn had the burndown up on the big screen in the sim bay, through the end of Wednesday.

Sprint A2-2 burndown: points remaining at the end of each day. Committed: 32 points over ten working days, Monday, October 24 to Friday, November 4. On day 8, Wednesday, five points of new work were added for the descent defect, and five points were finished. Left: the descent hover story, 5; safe mode, second slice (Breather thermal hold), 8; the downlink summary, 3; a constants cleanup, 1. Full regression on the rig takes twenty two hours.
Seventeen left and two days, Rafa said. And twenty two hours of regression that has to start by two this afternoon to be done by noon tomorrow. We're not going to make it.
Garrett, on the speaker: Run the new tests. The full suite passed two weeks ago. Nothing that old has changed.
The descent fix touched the constants file, Mokoena said. Everything reads the constants file.
Haddad was at Watkins on Thursdays now. She was standing by the door with a cardboard tray of coffee she'd brought for the squad, and she hadn't put it down.
Seventeen points are left with two days to go. What should Sam do?
A. Ask the squad to work late tonight and tomorrow, with the regression running alongside on the rig.
B. Extend the sprint to next Wednesday, and move the review to give all committed work full regression.
C. Run only the new tests for Friday's review, and pick up the full regression in the next sprint.
D. Sit down with Haddad and agree which stories come out of the sprint, with done kept as it is.

Haddad puts the coffee down and they walk the burndown together. The descent hover is one integrated run from done, so its five points can finish before the regression has to start. She picks the descent hover, because it's the one the release can't do without and because the board's clerk will be watching for it. The second slice of safe mode, the Breather thermal hold, eight points, goes back to the top of the backlog for A2-3. So does the downlink summary, and the one point cleanup with it. The regression starts at 1:50. On Friday the squad shows twenty five points done, a smaller number than anybody wanted, and Haddad tells the room why before Rafa can. We found a defect on Tuesday, and we didn't hide it. That's what we did this sprint. It's what I'd want done on my ship.

That's a go. During a sprint, scope can be renegotiated with the product owner as the team learns. Quality can't drop. Read the burndown honestly, keep the definition of done, decide with the product owner what comes out, and show the increment you actually built.

Friday, November 4. At the review at two, before anything else, Rafa had flown the departure burn in the integrated sim twice, back to back, and it had flown twice. Afterward he wrote TWICE under ONCE on the sim bay door, smaller, and nobody said anything about it, which was how the squad celebrated.

3:30 PM, the retrospective, in the sim bay with the lights up. The squad, Haddad, Mokoena, Quinn, and two of Hana's engineers, because the constants file belonged to propulsion as much as anybody. Sam stood at the back by the door with his arms folded, because it wasn't his meeting.

Somebody had already written the defect's history on the whiteboard in a neat column, from the request to Furrow on Tuesday, October 25, to the run on Tuesday, November 1. Seven steps. At every one of them, somebody could have caught it.
Sam's defect report had gone to the board's clerk on Wednesday morning. The clerk had acknowledged it in capitals and put it on the agenda for the board's November session.
Garrett had sent one line at noon. Make sure we know who signed off on it.
Garrett wants to know who signed off on the routine. What's Sam's best move after the defect?
A. Write up the lessons learned with the timeline and the fix, and file them in the program's register.
B. Use the retrospective to establish who approved the merge and who skipped the review.
C. Run a blameless retrospective on the defect, and send the fixes to the company's software standard.
D. Skip this sprint's retrospective, and leave the defect to its own report and review.

They go down the column one step at a time, asking what made each step reasonable when it happened, and never who. The answers are ordinary and damning. The example Furrow was given came from Earth. The tests came from the same example. The review checklist had no line for constants. The outside review came after the integrated run, when it came at all. By five they have four changes, and Quinn writes them on one page. Every line of AI generated flight code is marked in its commit and reviewed by a named person who can explain it. Its tests are written from the requirement by somebody who didn't generate it. Constants come from the one program file and are never typed in. And Furrow stays, for what it's good at, which is a lot. The page goes into Tallgrass's software standard on Monday as revision 12, to every program in the company, and up to the station in the morning packet. The station's reply is one line. Q4. Understood as: you found it, and you told us how. We'd like to use this for the station's code. At 5:10 Sam answers Garrett's message from noon. All of us. It's fixed now.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. A blameless retrospective looks for the conditions that made a mistake easy, not the person who made it, so people keep bringing problems forward. Then the lessons go somewhere that outlasts the team: the organization's standards and process assets, shared with everyone who could make the same mistake.

Wednesday, November 16. The Independent Readiness Board's November session was in the room in the federal building downtown, with the same bad coffee and the same terrazzo in the hall. Item three on the agenda was a demonstration of the autonomy release, requested by the board, in a form left to the program. The sim bay couldn't come downtown, so there'd be a live link.

Garrett's office had a video ready: run one, from September, cut to four minutes with music under it. Hale's chief of staff had seen it and liked it. Rafa had a deck of velocity charts and burndowns, all of them honest. Mokoena had stopped by Sam's office on Monday with one question. What are you going to show them? The ship, or the team?
The full regression had run with the descent fix in it before the code went anywhere near a release. The squad had stopped talking about it, which Sam took as a good sign.
The containment had held. Every line Furrow had written since July had been read, by the squad and by Mokoena's team together, and the board had had Sam's report for two weeks.
Ruth was at the end of the bench with her green pen, three seats from the chair. She hadn't looked at him when he came in. She never did, in that room.
Item three on the board's agenda is the autonomy demonstration. How should Sam handle it?
A. Show Garrett's four minute video of run one, the cleanest flight from September.
B. Ask the board to postpone the demonstration until the release is complete.
C. Present the squad's velocity and burndown charts against its forecast for the release.
D. Fly today's build live in the integrated sim, including the parts that still fail.

The link opens at ten. Rafa runs it from the sim bay, with Haddad in the left seat and her hands in her lap. Departure, clean. Coast, clean. Capture at Mars, crude, and it works. Then the descent, which hovers at thirty percent, and then fails the translate, on screen, in front of a federal board, because the translate is two sprints away. Rafa says so. Sam tells the defect story in four minutes: Earth's gravity in a Mars lander, a tool that did what it was shown, a review that didn't read the number, and what the squad did about it. Member Calder asks one question. How many times has it flown? The departure, twice in a row. The rest, once each. That's what we've got. She writes it down. That afternoon the board's questions go into the backlog, eleven of them, ordered by Haddad, with the board named as the requester.

Exactly right. Demonstrate value with the working increment, in front of the people who decide, as it really is. A sprint review is a working session: show what works and what doesn't, say what you learned, and turn the stakeholders' feedback into backlog items.

Monday, November 21. Page seven came in the mail on a gray afternoon with a Golden postmark, and the first snow of the season blowing sideways across the porch in Aurora. He read it at the kitchen table with his coat still on.
MAR 21 0930 ADMINISTRATOR ON THE LOOP: GOOD CALL, RUTHIE.

He read the 0715 line four times. APPROVED NEW TESTS ONLY. On November 3 he'd had his own version of that line, with smaller numbers in it, and Haddad had taken stories out of the sprint instead, and the squad had shown twenty five points to a room that wanted thirty two. It hadn't felt like a good call. It had felt like a Thursday.

The board's November minutes had a paragraph on the defect under the program's report, and a line at the end of it in the board's capitals: THE BOARD NOTES THAT THE PROGRAM'S REPORT WAS RECEIVED BEFORE ANY INQUIRY.
Tallgrass's software standard was at revision 12. Three other programs in the building had asked for the page, and one of them had found a constant of its own.

Haddad's card was still at the top of the governance column. CRITERIA FOR AN UNCREWED DEPARTURE. By Thanksgiving she'd written four of them with her crew, at her kitchen table in Aurora, and sent them to the board for its December session. The first one said: Only if no crew can go.

Ada's answer had come on October 19. Malik called his mom. He said she asked him how he was, and then she waited, and he told her. He's still coughing. She's still on Earth. But he's less alone with it, and so am I, and I didn't break a promise. Thanks for not making me.

On Quinn's integrated plan there was a milestone that hadn't been there in September, a diamond with a dashed line and the word OPTION beside it in capitals, Hana's word. Release A2, most likely February 24, range February 10 to March 10. It was the only thing on the plan that existed in case.

Thursday, November 24. Thanksgiving. He'd been asked to three houses and gone to none of them. At eight he sat at the kitchen table with a plate from the grocery store's hot counter and pressed record. One way light time fifteen minutes and thirty seconds. He told her about page seven, and Field 6, and the gravity constant, which she'd appreciate, because at twelve she'd lost a science fair to a units error and cried about it in the car all the way home.
He told her it had been a good two months, mostly, and then he told her the parts that hadn't been, because she'd ask.
He didn't do the voice. He sent it, and fifteen minutes and thirty seconds later it was on Mars.
Monday, November 28. 8:05 AM. Peg Sato came into his office without knocking, which she'd never done, put a folder on his desk, and sat down, which she'd also never done.
The folder was Aldergrove Fluid Systems blue, with the Pueblo address on the label. Inside was a letter on the company's letterhead, signed by Nell Garrity, requesting a change to the valve contract.

Aldergrove wants the root cause work pulled out of their fixed price. They put a number on it. I've read the number twice, once sitting down. She folded her glasses and set them on the folder. Garrett called me at six. He'd like to fire them.

Sam opened the folder. Under the letter somebody at Aldergrove had clipped a photocopy of a page from 2034, cold cycle data in faded columns, and beside the third row, in Nell's handwriting, two words: Still asking. He closed it again and put his hand flat on the cover, the way Quinn did, and thought about who in the building he had to talk to first. It wasn't Garrett.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 447. In the morning it would say 446, folder or no folder.
